primer.text: From Alkenes you already know the C=C double bond opens to add new atoms. This note runs the classic classroom reaction: bromine adding across that bond to give dibromoalkanes, and the same chemistry in water form as the orange bromine water test that tells alkenes from alkanes in one shake.

lessons.title: Bromine adds across the double bond
lessons.opening: Alkenes take simple molecules onto their double bond, and bromine is the textbook partner. This lesson watches bromine add across C=C and generalises the move to every halogen and alkene pair.
keyPoints: Alkenes undergo addition reactions in which atoms add across the C=C double bond.
When bromine reacts with an alkene, a dibromoalkane is formed.
Bromine plus ethene gives dibromoethane, with one bromine on each of the two carbons.
The same addition works for any halogen with any alkene, atoms always adding across the C=C.
No other products form: both bromine atoms end up bonded, one to each carbon of the old double bond.

low.restatement: Bromine does not need UV light with an alkene: the double bond simply opens and one bromine atom attaches to each carbon. The single product is a dibromoalkane. The alkene offers the open bond, so the halogen needs no light at all.
low.analogy: The double bond is a two-seat bench that is reserved; bromine arrives and both seats fill at once, one bromine per carbon, no queue left over.
low.examPointer: Say addition across the C=C, and remember no UV condition and no second product apply here.

medium.restatement: In an addition reaction the atoms of a simple molecule add across the C=C double bond of an alkene, so bromine and ethene form dibromoethane with each carbon gaining one bromine. The move generalises to any halogen with any alkene, always yielding one product where both halogen atoms bond across the former double bond.
medium.analogy: Picture a drawbridge that lowers to let two riders cross side by side: the double bond opens, each carbon hosts one halogen rider, and the bridge closes as single bonds again.
medium.examPointer: Write the dibromoalkane product with a bromine on each carbon, and state the reaction type as addition with no other products.

check.stem: What type of reaction occurs between ethene and bromine?

options.text: Addition, with both bromine atoms adding across the double bond
options.explanation: The C=C opens, both atoms attach, and a single dibromoethane product forms.

options.text: Substitution, needing ultraviolet light
options.explanation: Substitution under UV is the alkane route; the alkene adds instead with no light needed.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is reactive
options.explanation: Combustion burns in oxygen; bromine is not oxygen.

options.text: No reaction occurs at room temperature
options.explanation: The double bond reacts immediately, decolourising the bromine.

check.stem: What product forms when bromine adds to ethene?

options.text: Dibromoethane, with one bromine on each carbon
options.explanation: C2H4Br2 carries one bromine per carbon across the opened double bond.

options.text: Bromoethane and hydrogen bromide
options.explanation: That pair would be a substitution pattern; no hydrogen leaves ethene here.

options.text: Ethanol and water
options.explanation: Oxygen compounds belong to other chemistry entirely.

options.text: Ethene and bromine unchanged
options.explanation: The addition is fast and complete at room temperature.

check.stem: Why does no UV light condition appear in the alkene-bromine reaction?

options.text: Because the openable double bond reacts without any light trigger
options.explanation: The C=C provides the reactive handle that alkanes lack, so no UV initiation is needed.

options.text: Because UV light would stop the reaction
options.explanation: UV is simply unnecessary here, not an inhibitor.

options.text: Because bromine produces its own light
options.explanation: Bromine water is just orange; no self-illumination exists.

options.text: Because the reaction only happens in darkness
options.explanation: Light presence is irrelevant; the double bond does the work.

check.stem: How many products leave an alkene-halogen addition reaction?

options.text: One, the dibromoalkane or equivalent dihalide
options.explanation: Everything that enters ends up inside the single addition product.

options.text: Two, as in the alkane substitution
options.explanation: Two products signal substitution; addition merges everything into one.

options.text: Three, one per bond broken
options.explanation: Only the double bond converts to singles; no third product appears.

options.text: It depends on the alkene chain length
options.explanation: Chain length changes the formula, never the single-product pattern.

check.stem: Bromine is reacted with propene instead of ethene. What forms?

options.text: A dibromopropane, with bromines across the former double bond
options.explanation: Any alkene takes the same addition, so the three-carbon chain gains two bromines.

options.text: Nothing, because only ethene reacts
options.explanation: The note generalises the reaction to any alkene.

options.text: Dibromoethane, one carbon short
options.explanation: Atom conservation forbids losing the third carbon of propene.

options.text: Bromopropane plus hydrogen bromide
options.explanation: That single-bromo plus HBr pattern belongs to alkane substitution.

lessons.title: The bromine water test
lessons.opening: The same addition chemistry becomes a laboratory test when the bromine is dissolved in water. This lesson follows the orange colour through both outcomes and explains why the difference appears.
keyPoints: Bromine water is an orange solution used to test for alkenes, being safer than bromine itself.
Added to an alkane, bromine water stays orange because there is no C=C bond for the bromine to add across.
With an alkene, the bromine joins onto the double bond and the orange colour fades away.
The decolourising happens because free bromine no longer remains in the solution.
The test works because alkanes are saturated and alkenes are unsaturated, so only the alkene reacts.

low.restatement: Shake bromine water with the unknown liquid. Orange staying means an alkane; orange vanishing means an alkene whose double bond swallowed the bromine. One shake of the tube settles the question of which family the liquid belongs to.
low.analogy: The orange colour is a queue of bromine molecules waiting for work; an alkene gives them a job and the queue empties, while an alkane leaves them standing around.
low.examPointer: Record both outcomes in full: stays orange for the alkane, decolourises for the alkene.

medium.restatement: Bromine water, an orange solution safer to handle than bromine, distinguishes saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons. With an alkane it remains orange because no double bond exists to accept bromine; with an alkene the bromine adds across the C=C, free bromine is used up, and the solution decolourises.
medium.analogy: Bromine water is an orange-clothed inspector: with an alkane it finds no door to enter and stays visibly dressed, but at a double bond it enters the building and comes out in plain clothes.
medium.examPointer: Explain the colour loss mechanistically, bromine atoms adding across C=C leaving no free bromine, rather than just naming the colours.

check.stem: Why is bromine water used instead of pure bromine for the test?

options.text: Because it is safer and easier to handle than bromine
options.explanation: The note gives safety and ease of handling as the reasons for the aqueous form.

options.text: Because pure bromine cannot react with alkenes
options.explanation: Pure bromine reacts even faster; the water form is chosen for safety.

options.text: Because water is needed as a catalyst
options.explanation: Water is a solvent here, not a catalyst.

options.text: Because bromine is colourless on its own
options.explanation: Bromine is strongly coloured; that is where the test colour comes from.

check.stem: What is observed when bromine water is shaken with hexane, an alkane?

options.text: The solution stays orange
options.explanation: With no C=C bond available, the bromine remains free in solution and coloured.

options.text: The solution decolourises immediately
options.explanation: Decolourising is the alkene outcome; the alkane cannot accept the bromine.

options.text: The mixture turns blue
options.explanation: No blue species forms in this test at any point.

options.text: The bromine water boils off
options.explanation: Gentle shaking causes no boiling; the observation is about colour.

check.stem: Why does bromine water decolourise when added to an alkene?

options.text: The bromine atoms add across the C=C bond, leaving no free bromine in solution
options.explanation: Consumed bromine cannot colour the solution, so the orange fades away.

options.text: The alkene bleaches the water by dilution
options.explanation: Dilution does not consume the bromine; the addition reaction does.

options.text: The alkene burns the bromine away
options.explanation: Nothing burns; no oxygen or flame is involved.

options.text: The colour sinks to the bottom as a solid
options.explanation: The bromine becomes bonded into the organic molecule, not a precipitate.

check.stem: A hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water rapidly at room temperature. What does this show?

options.text: The hydrocarbon is an alkene with a C=C double bond
options.explanation: Rapid decolourising without UV is the signature of the unsaturated alkene.

options.text: The hydrocarbon is an alkane
options.explanation: Alkanes leave bromine water orange; only unsaturation decolourises it.

options.text: The hydrocarbon must contain oxygen
options.explanation: The test reads C=C unsaturation and says nothing about oxygen.

options.text: The sample must be heated before testing
options.explanation: The result already occurred at room temperature, which is the point of the test.

check.stem: Why does the C=C bond make alkenes more reactive than alkanes towards bromine?

options.text: The double bond has high electron density that invites attack and can open
options.explanation: The exam hint ties alkene reactivity to the electron-rich, openable double bond.

options.text: Because alkenes are smaller molecules
options.explanation: Size is not the driver; the bonding is.

options.text: Because alkenes dissolve bromine water better
options.explanation: Solubility is not the chemistry; addition across C=C is.

options.text: Because alkanes repel bromine strongly
options.explanation: Alkanes do not repel bromine; they simply offer no bond to react with.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which atoms add across the C=C double bond of an alkene, forming one product.
The product of adding bromine across an alkene double bond, with one bromine on each carbon.
The orange aqueous solution of bromine used to test for unsaturation, safer than bromine itself.
To lose colour; bromine water decolourises when its bromine adds across a C=C bond.
The concentration of electrons in a bond; the C=C bond is electron-rich and open to attack.

workedExample.prompt: a) Write the equation for ethene reacting with bromine, naming the product and the reaction type. b) State the observation when bromine water is shaken with hexane (an alkane) and explain it. c) State the observation with an alkene and explain why the colour fades.
steps: a) C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2: an addition reaction in which both bromine atoms add across the C=C double bond, forming dibromoethane as the only product.
b) Bromine water stays orange: alkanes have no C=C bond, so the bromine has nowhere to add and remains free in solution.
c) The orange colour decolourises: the bromine atoms add across the alkene's C=C bond, so no free bromine is left in solution.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2 (addition; dibromoethane). b) Stays orange — no C=C for addition. c) Decolourises — bromine adds across the double bond.
